questions.question: What two ingredients are needed for a semigroup?
options: A set and any binary operation, associative or not.
A set and a commutative binary operation on it.
A set and an associative binary operation on it.
A set and a binary operation that has an identity.

questions.question: Does a semigroup have to contain an identity element?
options: No. An identity is not required for a semigroup.
Yes, and every element must also be invertible.
No, because semigroups are not allowed to have binary operations.
Yes. Every semigroup is automatically a monoid.

questions.question: Why are products such as $a\star b\star c$ unambiguous in a semigroup?
options: Every element is its own inverse.
The operation is associative.
The set has exactly three elements.
The operation is necessarily commutative.

questions.question: Which larger structures are automatically semigroups?
options: Only sets with no operation.
Only vector spaces.
Monoids and groups.
Only fields.

questions.question: Is commutativity part of the definition of a semigroup?
options: Only if the set is infinite.
No. A semigroup may be noncommutative.
Yes. Semigroup operations must be commutative.
No, because semigroups cannot be associative.

questions.question: Why is every group also a semigroup?
options: A group's operation is associative, as a semigroup requires.
A group's operation is commutative, as a semigroup requires.
A group has inverses, and inverses imply associativity.
A group's identity element is what makes it a semigroup.

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb{Z},-)$ not a semigroup?
options: Subtraction has an identity element.
Subtraction is not closed on $\mathbb{Z}$.
The integers are not a set.
Subtraction is not associative.

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb{N},+)$ a semigroup?
options: Addition is closed on $\mathbb{N}$ and associative
Every natural number has an additive inverse in $\mathbb{N}$
Multiplication on $\mathbb{N}$ is commutative
A semigroup must contain an identity element

questions.question: For $n\times n$ real matrices under multiplication, what semigroup property is being used?
options: Matrix multiplication is commutative on square matrices.
Square matrices are closed under multiplication only if invertible.
Matrix multiplication is associative on square matrices.
Every $n\times n$ matrix has an inverse under multiplication.

questions.question: On $\mathbb{R}$, is $a\star b=\max(a,b)$ a semigroup operation?
options: Only if the operation is not commutative.
No, because maximum is not closed on $\mathbb{R}$.
No, because maximum has no inverse for every element.
Yes, maximum is closed and associative.

questions.question: What is the smallest algebraic demand that distinguishes a semigroup from a bare binary operation?
options: Associativity.
Existence of scalar multiplication.
Commutativity.
Existence of inverses.

questions.question: Why is every group a semigroup?
options: A group operation has an identity, as semigroups need.
A group operation is closed, which is all a semigroup needs.
A group operation is associative and binary.
Every semigroup has inverses, just as a group does.

questions.question: What can a semigroup lack that a monoid must have?
options: Associativity.
An identity element.
A binary operation.
Inverses for every element.

questions.question: On a set $A$, define $a\star b=a$. Does this make $A$ a semigroup?
options: Yes, the operation is associative.
No, because the operation is not closed.
No, because the operation ignores $b$.
No, unless $A$ has an identity element.

questions.question: Why are all $2\times3$ matrices not a semigroup under ordinary matrix multiplication?
options: The product is defined but not associative.
The product of two $2\times3$ matrices is a $2\times2$ matrix.
Non-square matrices have no identity, so no semigroup exists.
The product of two $2\times3$ matrices is not defined.

questions.question: On positive integers, is multiplication a semigroup operation?
options: Yes, because every positive integer $n$ has an inverse $1/n$ in the set.
No, because not every positive integer has a multiplicative inverse.
Yes; the set is closed under multiplication, which is associative.
No, because $1$ is an identity, which a semigroup cannot have.

questions.question: Why does a semigroup not automatically allow equations like $a\star x=b$ to be solved?
options: A semigroup has no binary operation.
Closure fails in every semigroup.
Associativity prevents equations from having solutions.
Inverses are not part of the semigroup axioms.

questions.question: Can a semigroup be commutative?
options: Yes, and then it automatically becomes a group.
No, semigroups are defined to be noncommutative.
Yes, but commutativity is optional.
Only if it has no associative law.

questions.question: On positive natural numbers, is $(\mathbb{N},+)$ a semigroup but not a monoid?
options: No, because $1$ serves as the identity for addition there.
No, because it lacks inverses, so it is not even a semigroup.
Yes; addition is associative there, but it fails to be commutative.
Yes; addition is associative there, but the identity $0$ is missing.

questions.question: Let $a\star b=a+b+1$ on $\mathbb{Z}$. What structure does this operation at least give?
options: Not a semigroup, because it has an identity.
Not a semigroup, because the $+1$ breaks associativity.
A semigroup: the operation is closed and associative.
Not a semigroup, because it is commutative.
